rv.q: Daisy Edgar-Jones is truly phenomenal as Maggie, the complicated female lead of Cat on a Hot Tin Roof.
Frecknall is unsurpassed at stripping away accumulated frippery from Williams's work and honing in unrelentingly on the undercurrents of emotion.
It is a striking and vivid interpretation that makes a hazily-remembered classic feel new and strange.
It comes across as epic and often magnificent.

In perhaps the best scene here, it’s Big Daddy who forces Brick to fully acknowledge this truth and somehow Ben-Adir, in a deeply compassionate performance, makes sense of Brick’s anachronistic abject self-loathing within a modern setting.
What you can’t really feel, though, is the hum of desperate sexual frustration.
Lennie James’s Big Daddy is physically unimposing but he makes a larger-than-life tyrant, lusting for life even in the face of death.
But as it builds, Rebecca Frecknall’s star-filled staging finds a queer kind of power.
For all his virtues, James can’t stop a long evening slipping into mannered excess.
Here’s a production which uncomfortably captures that anguish.
James brings extraordinary subtlety and tenderness to a character who is too often a simple bully.

Here, Kingsley Ben-Adir and Lennie James provide a riveting hour of drama, a duologue also filled with circularity but one that incrementally chips away at the reserves of both men who see one another fully for the first time in all their flawed, broken honesty.
While the cast are compelling they’re restricted by odd directorial and dramaturgical choices that leave the show coming across as juvenile and one-dimensional.

cn.t: Mixed reviews greet Frecknall's Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, with Edgar-Jones's Maggie drawing both praise and skepticism. Most critics admire her fierce physicality, though some find the production overlong and emotionally uneven.
